rule.title: Boundary Request Validation via Zod Schemas
rule.statement: All incoming HTTP requests (body, query, params) must be validated by Zod schemas in middleware before touching controller logic.
rule.rationale: Unvalidated input is the root cause of injection attacks, data corruption, and unhandled runtime exceptions in downstream services.
rule.implementation_guidance: Attach a validate(schema) middleware to every Express route. Reject invalid requests with HTTP 422.

forbidden.example: Accessing req.body.documentTitle inside the controller without schema validation.

source.evidence_quote: Validation must occur at the boundary of the API. Any input that does not conform to the strict schema must be rejected immediately before processing.

rule.title: Strict Rejection of Unknown Request Fields
rule.statement: Validation schemas must strip or strictly reject unrecognized fields to prevent mass assignment vulnerabilities.
rule.rationale: Attackers can submit unexpected fields (e.g., isAdmin: true) that, if passed directly to database models, compromise security.
rule.implementation_guidance: Use zodSchema.strict() or ensure Prisma update payloads only use parsed, typed properties.

forbidden.example: await prisma.user.update({ where: { id }, data: req.body }); // Mass assignment vulnerability

source.evidence_quote: Mass assignment occurs when a client binds HTTP request parameters directly into data objects. Strict schemas must disallow unexpected properties.

rule.title: Active Idempotency Deduplication Execution
rule.statement: Endpoints receiving mutation requests with an Idempotency-Key must actively query for existing records using fast-path caching or double-checked locking inside database transactions, returning the cached result (HTTP 200) instead of re-executing mutations. Validating and storing the key without duplicate querying is strictly forbidden as decorative security.
rule.rationale: Merely validating the UUID format and storing the key in the database provides zero double-spend protection. Clients retrying requests after network timeouts will trigger duplicate financial debits if the service does not actively intercept duplicates before mutating state.
rule.implementation_guidance: Check for an existing completed transaction by idempotency key before entering the critical mutation block. If found, return the cached transfer result with isIdempotentReplay: true. Within transactions, use unique constraints on idempotency_key to guarantee database-level atomicity.

forbidden.example: Validating idempotencyKey with Zod and passing it to repository.createTransferRecord() without any findByIdempotencyKey() check.

preferred.example: const existing = await repo.findByIdempotencyKey(key); if (existing) return formatExistingResult(existing);

source.book_title: Design and Build Great Web APIs
source.evidence_quote: An idempotency key allows clients to safely retry requests without fear of performing the same operation twice. The server must check for the presence of the key in prior transactions before executing state modifications.
